entries.content:
Pankaj Bajpai

Cloud Data Engineer

Abhilash Adavi

AI Engineer

Enterprise AI needs to go beyond simple chat interfaces. To provide real value, AI agents must access your data warehouses to generate actionable insights, all while maintaining strict security and data governance.

This guide explores how to build a secure bridge between Google Cloud’s Gemini Enterprise and Snowflake. By using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and the Google Agent Development Kit (ADK), you can empower your agent to act as an assistant that understands natural language, generates precise SQL via Snowflake Cortex and executes queries with user-level permissions.

Choosing the right integration pattern

Direct Connection vs. custom orchestration

The Google ADK architecture demonstrated in this post represents the advanced / custom orchestration pattern. It is designed for developers building complex, multi-agent systems on Google Cloud, such as workflows that combine Snowflake insights with external enterprise tools, custom reasoning loops, or cross-platform state management in Gemini Agent Engine.

For standard enterprise basic use cases where you want to connect Gemini Enterprise directly to Snowflake use the joint solutions mentioned in this link.

The architectural approach

This architecture allows a business user to ask questions like, "What were our top 5 selling items in Texas last quarter?"

Rather than exposing raw SQL execution to the client, the agent delegates both query generation and execution to a governed Snowflake Cortex Agent exposed through the Snowflake MCP server:

  • Governed translation: The ADK agent passes the user's natural language question to the Snowflake MCP server, which invokes the Cortex Agent (CORTEX_AGENT_RUN) backed by Cortex Analyst semantic view.
  • Direct execution within the governed boundary: The Cortex Agent translates the question into SQL and executes it directly inside Snowflake using the authenticated user's OAuth session and role privileges, returning the structured results to the ADK agent.

This approach provides deterministic text-to-SQL translation mapped to your corporate semantic definitions, keeps query execution inside Snowflake's governed boundary, and reduces the risk of schema hallucinations or unvalidated SQL execution.

System architecture flow

The diagram below illustrates the trust boundaries and the numbered flow of execution between the Gemini Enterprise app and Snowflake ecosystems.

Detailed execution sequence

To highlight how the agent delegates natural language query translation and governed execution to the Snowflake Cortex Agent over MCP, see the sequence diagram below:

Step 1: Setting up the Snowflake security integration

A major risk in enterprise AI is granting the model broad access via a generic service account, which could allow users to bypass security restrictions. We solve this by using OAuth 2.0 to perform user impersonation.

First, establish a confidential OAuth client in Snowflake to protect the client secret. The snippet below configures the security integration inside Snowflake:

Step 2: Data governance and access control

Apply the principle of least privilege by creating a dedicated role for your agent inside Snowflake.

IMPORTANT

  • The user context must have SELECT privileges on the physical tables backing the semantic view. Granting access only to the semantic view will cause runtime errors during query execution.
  • If granting direct access to base tables is not permitted by your security policy, place a Snowflake Secure View over the physical tables and build the Semantic View on top of it. Because Snowflake views execute with Owner's Rights, the user's GenAI role only needs SELECT privileges on the Secure View and Semantic View rather than the raw tables.
  • Snowflake OAuth tokens capture and bind to the user's DEFAULT_ROLE and DEFAULT_WAREHOUSE at the exact moment of authorization. If a user authorizes the connection before these defaults are configured, the session will be locked to the wrong role(role available at that time) and query execution will fail if the intended role will not have required privileges.
    • Set defaults(as shown below) prior to authorizing in Gemini Enterprise.
    • Authorize connection: Have the user perform the one-time OAuth authorization in Gemini Enterprise.
    • (Optional) Revert defaults: Once authorized, the user can safely revert their default role and warehouse in Snowflake back to their standard operational preferences.

Step 3: Provisioning the Cortex Agent and MCP server inside Snowflake

Next, create a governed Cortex Agent in Snowflake using your semantic view, then provision an MCP server that exposes the agent via the CORTEX_AGENT_RUN tool type. This approach delegates both SQL generation and query execution to Snowflake while enforcing the caller's OAuth identity and role permissions.

ISOLATION & GOVERNANCE NOTE: By using CORTEX_AGENT_RUN, query generation and execution remain fully contained within Snowflake's governed security boundary. Avoid exposing raw execution tools like SYSTEM_EXECUTE_SQL to external clients, as doing so introduces unnecessary security surface area and bypasses centralized Cortex Agent governance.

Depending on your organization's specific requirements, you should add robustness on top of this template (e.g., custom error handling, structured schemas, custom prompts, configurations, and additional tool wrappers).

Step 6: Project structure and deployment

2. Deploying via the CLI

Rather than running complex custom Python scripts or manual container builds, you can deploy using the official Google Agents CLI (agents-cli). The CLI packages your code, sets up the server, and handles the deployment pipeline:

The CLI automatically handles the deployment lifecycle. Once complete, it outputs the unique project resource path (e.g., projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/reasoningEngines/RESOURCE_ID) which you will use to register the agent in the next step.

TIP: For more information and advanced configuration options for ADK agent deployment, refer to:

Step 7: Registering the custom agent in Gemini Enterprise

Once the agent code is ready and deployed, register the agent in the Google Cloud Console. Here, you will link the agent configuration and map the OAuth parameters retrieved from your Snowflake Security Integration.

  • Extracting the OAuth Endpoints from Snowflake

Run this query in Snowflake to extract the precise Token and Authorization endpoints:

In the results, locate the values for the following properties:

  • OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_ENDPOINT: Your Snowflake Authorization URI.
  • OAUTH_TOKEN_ENDPOINT: Your Snowflake Token URI.

2. Registration steps in Google Cloud console

  • Go to the Gemini Enterprise page in the console.
  • Select the application you want to register the agent with.
  • In the left navigation, click Agents, then click + Add agent.
  • Select Add for Custom agent via Agent Platform. The Authorizations setup displays.
  • Set up the Snowflake OAuth connection:
    • Click Add authorization.
    • Authorization name: Enter the exact ID you defined in your ADK code (e.g., snowflake_oauth_conn). This ensures the credentials map correctly to the code's AUTH_ID.
    • Client ID & Client secret: Input the credentials you retrieved from Snowflake using the SYSTEM$SHOW_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRETS query.
    • Token URI: Input the exact token endpoint value extracted from DESCRIBE SECURITY INTEGRATION.
    • Authorization URI: Take the authorization endpoint value extracted from DESCRIBE SECURITY INTEGRATION and append ?response_type=code at the end (along with your client ID and scope query parameters, for example):

IMPORTANT

Ensure the Authorization URI ends with &response_type=code (or ?response_type=code if there are no other parameters). This parameter is required by Google Cloud to trigger the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow.

  • Click Done, then click Next.

6. Configure the agent properties:

7. Click Create to complete registration.

Understanding identifier alignment

  • ADK Code AUTH_ID <==> Google Cloud Authorization Name: The AUTH_ID in your Python script must exactly match the Authorization Name/ID you input during console registration. Because we write code first, we reuse the code-defined identifier during registration.
  • Snowflake Security Integration Name (e.g. ): This is purely a Snowflake-side database object name. It does not need to match the Google Cloud Authorization Name or the AUTH_ID in your ADK Python code.

Get started

By uniting the Gemini model’s reasoning capabilities, ADK's orchestration, and Snowflake's governed data layer, you can safely bring AI to your data. This architecture provides an agentic assistant that respects your security perimeters while delivering business value.

entries.content:
Siddharth Deekshit

Product Manager

Surekha Balla

Senior Software Engineer

As organizations adopt autonomous agents to build applications, securing identities and access has become more challenging. Developers relying on agents to provision cloud resources, write Terraform, and deploy microservices at machine-speed only find their CI/CD pipelines blocked even faster as security friction scales.

To help you get ahead of agentic-era Identity and Access Management, today we’re introducing IAM Helper. This suite of intelligent, agent-facing building blocks can automate complex, end-to-end IAM workflows.

As an agent-native orchestration and interface layer for Google Cloud IAM, it augments Google Cloud’s core IAM engines — including Policy Intelligence and Privileged Access Manager (PAM) — making IAM skills callable directly by autonomous code assistants, deployment pipelines, and custom agents. Using this functionality reduces the administrative overhead of maintaining least-privilege security and agent governance, while maximizing utility, and accelerating deployment.

IAM Helper Agent Skills: Fast, secure deployment with automated governance

Manual troubleshooting of permission blockers creates friction for engineering and administrators, while shortcuts can lead to broad agent over-permissioning that puts least privilege at risk.

IAM Helper empowers agents to handle access management dynamically. It shifts the burden of policy evaluation away from human administrators and LLMs, offloading complex orchestration directly to the Google Cloud backend, to maximize token efficiency and prevent costly operational bottlenecks.

Rather than operating as isolated utilities, IAM Helper Agent Skills guide agents through the cloud access lifecycle. These end-to-end workflows, helper scripts, and guardrails packaged using the open Agent Skills standard can orchestrate multiple underlying functions and APIs to resolve complex IAM tasks. They work across common agents (Gemini CLI, Gemini Cloud Assist, ADK, Claude Code, and Cursor). 

Built-in guardrails and real-world impact

Every IAM Helper agent skill separates read-only discovery from policy changes: Diagnostics and simulations run automatically, while any change to access policies pauses for human-in-the-loop (HITL) confirmation based on customizable risk tiers. To see the value of IAM Helper in practice, consider how it transforms two everyday scenarios:

  • Scaled user-assisted remediation: Suppose a developer's coding agent hits a 403 error while deploying a new application. Rather than filing a support ticket and idling, the agent uses iam-helper-for-troubleshooting to identify the missing Pub/Sub permission in seconds, then uses iam-helper-for-privileged-access-management to request a one-hour JIT grant, eliminating hours of debugging friction.

  • Autonomous pipeline self-healing: An infrastructure agent encounters a permission block during a routine deployment pipeline. Rather than failing the build, the pipeline uses IAM Helper Agent skills to generate a revised, least-privilege policy, verifies against 90 days of logs via iam-helper-for-policy-simulator that active services won't break, and routes the change to an admin for quick approval.

IAM Helper Agent Skills are designed for maximum token and cost efficiency, allowing agents to execute multi-step administrative operations autonomously.

  • Authoring compliant, least-privilege policies: As DevOps engineers translate access requirements into JSON, YAML, or Terraform HCL, iam-helper-for-policy-management generates and validates IAM v1 allow bindings and IAM v2 deny rules. It automatically catches and blocks risky configs before they are applied, including public access (allUsers) and broad basic roles (roles/owner, roles/editor).

  • Unblocking 403 errors in seconds: When an on-call engineer or deployment agent hits a cryptic 403 PERMISSION_DENIED error, iam-helper-for-troubleshooting identifies the exact missing permission or blocking rule in seconds. It adapts to the user’s role: Developers can check if they can unblock themselves locally or generate a structured ticket for their administrator (Requester flow), while security administrators can trace inherited allow and v2 deny rules across organization, folder, and project hierarchies to resolve the issue (Resolver flow).

  • Simulating blast radius before rolling out changes: Before a platform engineer updates a policy or applies IAM Recommender role reductions, they need confidence that active workloads won't break. iam-helper-for-policy-simulator walks the agent through a structured plan, simulate, analyze, and apply flow, testing proposed changes against 90 days of historical access logs to confirm existing traffic won't be disrupted before any update takes effect.

  • Elevating access just-in-time instead of granting standing privileges: When responders or maintenance agents need temporary production access, iam-helper-for-privileged-access-management manages the lifecycle of on-demand credentials through Privileged Access Manager (PAM). It supports requester, administrator, and approver workflows so elevated access is audited, time-bound, and automatically revoked once the task is done.

While IAM Helper Agent Skills supply the high-level workflow logic, they are all based on a common set of foundational MCP Tools.

Powered by Google Cloud IAM MCP tools

Google Cloud IAM Helper MCP tools provide the backend connection through atomic, read-only functions exposed via Google-managed MCP servers across core IAM endpoints (Policy Troubleshooter, Policy Analyzer, Policy Simulator, and IAM v1/v2 APIs).

Rather than requiring teams to write custom API wrappers, MCP tools give agents a standard way to query the cloud backend and get exact answers without parsing verbose policy documents in the prompt, maximizing token efficiency. Agents can dynamically discover and invoke these tools to execute basic operations like checking permissions or listing roles when custom logic is required.

Because operations like hierarchy traversal, group expansion, and policy evaluation happen on dedicated IAM endpoints (spanning IAM v1 allow roles, IAM v2 deny, Policy Troubleshooter, and Policy Analyzer), skills run quickly and accurately with minimal token usage. Teams can also use these atomic MCP tools directly when writing their own custom Agent Skills, making it straightforward to combine Google Cloud's IAM capabilities with internal ticketing systems, custom compliance checks, and existing deployment pipelines.

Getting started

Accelerate your agentic workflows, reduce operational overhead, and bring intelligent, scalable security to your deployment pipelines. Start building with IAM Helper Agent skills today by exploring our Google Cloud Agent Skills Catalog and dive deeper with the official IAM documentation.

entries.content:
Karan Batta

Senior Vice President, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure

Gurmeet Goindi

Sr. Director, Product Management

As AI workloads scale across every industry, organizations need compute options that optimize throughput, latency, and unit economics across the AI lifecycle. To meet this demand, Oracle and Google Cloud are partnering to bring Google Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), making OCI the first hyperscaler outside Google to offer TPUs. Together, we will deploy TPU capacity on OCI starting in the calendar year 2027.

TPUs: Co-designed from silicon to software

Google built its first TPU more than ten years ago on a clear product thesis: co-designing custom silicon alongside optical networking, power delivery, liquid cooling, and compiler software yields gains in performance per watt and total cost of ownership that isolated components cannot match.

TPU v1 delivered 30x the throughput per watt of contemporary processors. Today, TPUs train and serve Gemini across Google's billion-user products, and the eighth-generation TPUs deliver up to 12.6 PFLOPS of native FP4 compute per chip, over 100x TPU v1's 92 TFLOPS at up to 2x the performance per watt of the previous generation. However, raw FLOPS alone do not determine customer economics across training and inference. For training, the governing metric is goodput; the percentage of time a cluster spends doing productive computation. For inference, the governing metrics are latency and cost per token. TPUs address both through system-level co-design.

By pairing on-die Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) routing with Optical Circuit Switching (OCS), the control plane detects hardware or link degradations and dynamically routes optical paths around faults in real time without job restarts, sustaining over 97% goodput across thousands of chips on large-scale training runs and high availability for production serving. Increased on-chip SRAM, more HBM capacity, and a new low-diameter interconnect topology that cuts network hops by more than 50% allow the latest generation TPUs to deliver up to 80% better performance per dollar for low-latency serving.

This hardware efficiency translates into product velocity when developers can adopt it without friction. Our recent announcements at the PyTorch Conference reinforce our commitment to making the Google TPU software ecosystem an open, developer-friendly environment for the PyTorch community. Notably, TorchTPU, our native PyTorch stack for Google TPUs, is now available as open source on GitHub. You can now train, serve, and deploy models on TPUs using the tools you already rely on, including vLLM, SGLang, llm-d, TorchTitan, Ray, TorchRec, Hugging Face, LiteRT.  

This portability lets teams assign each workload to the accelerator that delivers the lowest cost per token or fastest time to train, without rewriting model code. And with today’s announcement, they will soon be able to assign those workloads to TPUs on Google Cloud or Oracle infrastructure.

Expanding the AI infrastructure ecosystem with OCI

Even as TPU adoption on Google Cloud grows, the global demand for AI compute exceeds any single cloud provider's footprint.Bringing TPUs to OCI gives customers four distinct benefits:

  • Data centers engineered for AI density: Google's TPU systems are designed for direct liquid cooling at rack scale, and OCI's next-generation data centers are built for exactly that profile. Oracle delivers flexible, durable capacity that can shift between frontier model training and production inference as customer demand changes. Pairing TPU efficiency with Oracle’s innovative power and cooling approaches, helps bring energy-efficient AI-compute capacity online rapidly, and at global scale.

  • Secure, high-performance networking with Oracle Acceleron: While TPUs move chip-to-chip traffic over ICI and OCS, Oracle Acceleron provides the networking foundation that connects TPU capacity to the rest of OCI. Acceleron’s SmartNIC with hardware-level tenant isolation, High Performance Fabric, and Zero Trust Packet Routing moves data between Oracle databases, storage, and TPU clusters with high throughput and low latency, without taxing host compute and without weakening security boundaries.

  • Proximity to enterprise data: Oracle databases are often the system-of-record for enterprise organizations. Offering TPUs directly within OCI lets organizations run fine-tuning and inference next to their existing enterprise data without costly cross-cloud transfers.

  • Multi-architecture choice: Providing TPUs alongside GPUs inside OCI gives teams the flexibility to assign each AI workload stage to the optimal accelerator for cost and performance.

By bringing Google TPUs to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, Google Cloud and Oracle are opening up over a decade of purpose-built AI systems engineering to a broader ecosystem of builders. When customers have more choices of purpose-built compute across more clouds, the entire industry builds faster and operates more efficiently. We can’t wait to see what you build.

entries.content:
Carolina Parada

VP and Head of Deepmind Robotics

Adrian Jones

Applied AI Blackbelt

Earlier this year, we introduced Gemini Robotics 2 — our next-generation intelligence layer enabling robots to think, act, and adapt in the physical world. At the core of this breakthrough is Gemini Robotics Embodied Reasoning 2 (ER 2), a specialized Gemini model that serves as a robot’s high-level brain. Working across any robot embodiment — from stationary arms to full humanoids — Gemini Robotics ER 2 combines advanced spatial and temporal video understanding with long-horizon planning and built-in safety guardrails. This enables robots to converse naturally with humans, orchestrate low-level action models and hardware APIs, execute multi-minute tasks involving hundreds of decisions, and collaborate across multi-robot teams.

Today, we are bringing this same frontier embodied reasoning model to enterprise production environments: Gemini Robotics ER 2 is now available in public preview on the Gemini platform. For the first time, organizations can pair Google DeepMind’s latest embodied reasoning model for robotics with the enterprise-grade security, multi-agent orchestration, and end-to-end lifecycle management of Google Cloud — making it easier to simulate, evaluate, and deploy safe, adaptive physical AI at scale.

Powering physical agents for enterprise robotics

Gemini Robotics ER 2 transforms a robot into a physical agent. The model combines deep spatio-temporal reasoning and long-horizon planning, enabling robots to orchestrate steps to complete a task, self-correct, and generalize to novel situations. To build an agentic setup, developers can declare low-level control interfaces — like Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models or navigation APIs — as tools, and stream multimodal video, audio, or text directly into the model.

Here is what the model delivers for businesses building and operating robotics:

1. Physical task verification, understanding, and self-correction

In physical operations, a robot needs to know whether a step actually succeeded before moving on to the next one. Gemini Robotics ER 2 adapts to new and unfamiliar situations on the fly by reasoning over continuous video feeds. The model:

  • Classifies task progress into binary status, discrete categories, or continuous scores to improve real-time situational awareness and enable real-time adjustment or iteration on failed steps, without restarting an entire workflow.

  • Pinpoints the exact video frame where a critical event occurs (such as when to stop pouring a liquid) with 91.3% accuracy and a 0.96-second mean absolute frame distance, running at 4x the execution speed and a fraction of the compute cost of many larger model categories.

  • It advances our core spatial reasoning capability, including visual question answering and instrument reading. For example, it can read and interpret values across 10+ instrument categories including circular dials, sight glasses, digital displays, linear scales, rulers, and liquid thermometers directly from visual input.

2. One intelligence layer across any embodiments

Gemini Robotics ER 2 orchestrates robots of many shapes and sizes, scaling its intelligence from stationary arms and wheeled rovers to quadrupeds and complex forms. It also unlocks multi-robot collaboration, allowing different types of robots to share a semantic understanding of their workspace, divide labor, and hand off tasks to complete workflows a single machine could not do alone.

3. Agentic tool orchestration and natural language interaction

Gemini Robotics ER 2 thinks about what comes next while simultaneously orchestrating actions. Developers can declare low-level control interfaces — such as VLA models, navigation APIs, or custom functions — as tools across simulation, real-world robot control, or human tele-operation. Gemini Robotics ER 2 can orchestrate navigation and manipulator movement APIs from natural language commands, allowing the robot to explain its approach while performing an action, and letting operators redirect it without using technical language.

4. Build safe, adaptive physical agents in Google Cloud

Developers and enterprise teams use the Gemini platform to simulate, orchestrate, and manage physical agents, which are then deployed to run directly on physical robots at the edge using Google Cloud's scalable infrastructure:

  • Simulate fast: Test robot behaviors before touching hardware by running simulations in familiar environments like MuJoCo-Warp and NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Then generate synthetic scenarios with multimodal models and auto-label workcell imagery on the Gemini platform.

  • Train smart: Use Gemini Robotics ER 2's spatial pointing, moment finding, and progress classification to curate and label demonstration videos in Cloud Storage and BigQuery. Then train custom Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models through the Gemini platform, GKE, or Cluster Director.

  • Operate easily: Deploy Gemini Robotics ER 2 workflows on the Gemini platform with enterprise IAM, security controls, and built-in function calling. Offload latency-sensitive local workloads like SLAM and path planning to factory floors with Google Distributed Cloud, and stream fleet telemetry into BigQuery. Explore the full architecture in Google Cloud Physical AI solutions.

How customers are building with Gemini Robotics ER 2 in Gemini platform

“We’ve seen exponential growth in customers using AIVI-Learning every month, and Gemini Robotics ER 2 brings them even more value. Video changes what an inspection can be. Spot isn’t just checking whether something looks right in a moment in time, the ability to apply AI models to video opens a whole new world of possibilities.”

Marco da Silva, VP and General Manager of Spot at Boston Dynamics

“DeepReach AI is the real-world skills engine for physical AI. Our hardware and AI platform capture how skilled people work all over the world, and turn it into data flywheel for model training. Gemini Robotics ER 2 gives us accurate task understanding of every recording, to help us find data that matters most — faster and at a far greater scale.”

Chris Liu, Co-founder and CTO at DeepReach

“Advanced reasoning models have the potential to help robots interpret complex environments, plan actions and adapt to changing conditions, opening new possibilities for physical AI. Google’s Gemini Robotics ER 2 model represents an important step in this direction, and we’re excited to be working with Google on exploring how these emerging capabilities can shape the next generation of robotics compute platforms.”

Barrie Mullins, Senior Director of Arm Total Design for Physical AI, at Arm

“We aim to accelerate materials R&D workflows so our scientists can test more ideas, faster. Most lab automation today relies on rigid scripts for single, isolated tasks. By using Gemini Robotics ER 2, we are giving our robots the visual and physical flexibility to work with our existing infrastructure - whether that’s reading a touchscreen on a legacy microwave reactor that has no API, balancing and loading a centrifuge, or moving samples safely through a busy lab. This is the next level that we aspire to reach. This brings us much closer to self-driving labs that can run full experimental campaigns from synthesis to separation, freeing our researchers to focus on thinking up new ideas for discovering new materials.”

Prof. Loh Xian Jun, Executive Director at ASTAR Institute of Materials Research and Engineering (ASTAR IMRE) and Executive Director of MARVEL-AI”

Get started with Gemini Robotics ER 2 in Gemini platform

Developers and enterprise teams can start building with Gemini Robotics ER 2 today in preview via Model Garden in Gemini platform.

  • Build in Gemini platform: Visit the Gemini Robotics ER 2 documentation and pricing.

  • Explore the Developer Guides: Check out sample code and bidirectional streaming guides in the Gemini API Robotics documentation.

  • Read the Research: Dive into the benchmarks and safety technical report in the Google DeepMind Gemini Robotics ER 2 announcement.

  • Explore Physical AI on Google Cloud: Visit cloud.google.com/solutions/physical-ai and cloud.google.com/ai to learn how Google Cloud infrastructure supports simulation, training, and deployment.

entries.content:
Jim Kelly

Vice President, Federal, Google Public Sector

As NASA advances its Artemis program to send astronauts on increasingly difficult missions to explore more of the Moon, build a sustained human presence there with a Moon Base, and build on their foundation for the first crewed missions to Mars, crew safety and Earth-independent autonomy are paramount. An astronaut on a future deep space mission to Mars could face severe operational challenges—including round-trip communication latencies of up to 44 minutes, making real-time medical guidance for crew nearly impossible.

Last year, Google Public Sector shared progress on the development of the Crew Medical Officer Digital Assistant (CMO-DA) - an automated Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) designed to assist astronauts with real-time medical guidance in remote and isolated environments. Today, we are building on this innovation with the development of a proof-of-concept physical, robotic system that aims to support deep space missions and could assist astronauts during NASA missions.

Optimizing crew time and safety

The future Moon Base in the lunar South Pole region of the Moon is planned to support sustained human presence. Because every minute in space is a strictly limited resource, reducing the physical burden on astronauts to maximize their time for science and discovery is a top priority. To potentially address this challenge, NASA’s Human Research Program, Johnson Space Center Robotics Team, and the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) collaborated with Google Public Sector to develop a robotic system. By handling routine logistics, this system could free up astronauts to focus on what humans do best: complex science and discovery.

To maximize its utility for a lean crew, the robotic system is designed as a versatile "payload" handler capable of managing cargo, logistics, and equipment. When not needed for routine maintenance like organizing tools or securing compartments, it can pivot to medical support. For example, if an astronaut experiences severe back pain—a potential symptom of kidney stones—the robot could retrieve and prepare an ultrasound machine. This enables the human crew medical officer to focus entirely on analyzing the scan and treating the patient.

Adapting spatial awareness and vision-language-action models for robotic systems

Operating safely alongside humans in confined spacecraft is a complex challenge. Unlike factory robots in fixed, human-free environments, space systems utilizing Super Intelligence (SI) require flexible, human-directed tools to safely adapt to close quarters. Because they must also rely on limited sensory input like cameras, JPL is adapting satellite situational awareness intelligence tools—originally designed to track objects in orbit—to help the robotic system navigate and understand its 3D surroundings.

To test this safely at Johnson Space Center’s iMETRO facility, Google DeepMind’s MuJoCo simulator was used, which is an advanced physics engine that allows the SI to practice complex movements in a highly accurate virtual environment before touching real hardware. In a recent proof-of-concept technology demonstration, the robotic system was tasked with a complex "pick-and-place" maneuver to locate and move a medical bag. By implementing an "eye-to-hand" camera configuration for enhanced spatial awareness, the open-source Pi0 model—developed by Physical Intelligence on Google Cloud infrastructure— achieved an initial 85% baseline success rate in these early lab environments, providing a strong foundation for the next phase of rigorous training and safety refinement. Because vision-language-action (VLA) models connect language directly to physical movement, astronauts could direct the robotic system flexibly via standard English text prompts.

Space: the ultimate edge-computing environment

Processing these complex tasks requires significant computing power, which presents another hurdle: space is the ultimate edge computing environment. Spacecraft cannot rely on continuous connections to Earth-based data centers. To solve this, the Google team harnessed Google Cloud G4 instances to rapidly train the underlying models, fine-tuning the 4-billion parameter Pi0 model in just 2.5 hours. Crucially, they demonstrated that the fine-tuned models can then operate locally on compact, energy-efficient edge devices. Over the last two years, the team tested approximately 15 different edge computing devices to find ones that run efficiently on lightweight, low-power hardware required for future Mars missions.

Pioneering the future of crew safety and space exploration

Looking ahead, the ultimate goal is to build a robotic system that can execute a variety of tasks via simple voice instructions, under the astronauts’ direct supervision and command. For instance, the robot might be directed to assist with routine health monitoring—such as capturing basic vitals or simple ultrasounds—under the strict guidance of a human crew medical officer. This ensures astronauts receive the physical assistance they might not be able to perform by themselves, without ever replacing human decision-making.

This collaboration between Google Public Sector and NASA can help pave the way for increasingly difficult missions that push the bounds of scientific discovery.

entries.content:
Nathaniel Zollinger

CTO, Crypto Finance Group

Moritz Platt

Capital Markets Technology Manager, Google Cloud

Every day, countless financial transactions are interrupted by slow, expensive, and inflexible conventional payment systems. As a result, public commercial stablecoins like Tether, USDC, and PayPal USD have become increasingly popular by making it easy to move money efficiently with instant, 24/7 blockchain settlement.

Yet major regulated banks have largely kept such transactions at arm’s length; for these financial institutions, reserve-backed public stablecoins present numerous risks, including strict capital and liquidity requirements and unmanageable regulatory and operational uncertainty.

Indeed, banks don't want to adopt existing stablecoins. Instead, they need the speed and efficiency of tokenized currency built on the trusted economic foundations they’ve nurtured over years or even decades in business. That’s why many are now turning to Google Cloud Universal Ledger (GCUL). Rather than channeling public stablecoins, GCUL provides the secure infrastructure banks need to issue and settle tokenized deposits. That brings real-time, 24/7 programmable payments into commercial bank money while satisfying regulators and without disrupting core banking operations.

For many banks, this is a compelling vision, but adopting new payment technology and integrating it with core banking systems can seem to bank CTOs like a daunting undertaking. That’s particularly true as they face mounting demands for the engineering resources that keep their businesses running while also striving to stay compliant with new regulations. But with a blockchain purpose-built for financial services like GCUL, this is anything but a herculean task.

Looking to expand its offerings for an increasingly global clientele, Switzerland’s Crypto Finance Group wanted to show it could deploy payment innovations like this in just weeks. That was its inspiration for launching a digital payments infrastructure pilot that enabled instant account-to-account transfers between customers of two Swiss banks on the GCUL network. The pilot, which was designed to operate within one of the world's most demanding financial security frameworks, provided a blueprint for how any commercial bank can build on Google Cloud technology to fundamentally modernize its payment operations.

Pain points in today's payments landscape

In recent years, there’s been a marked proliferation of tokenized payment methods. But stablecoins have transformed this previously niche technology, by effectively resolving some of traditional finance’s most enduring pain points, such as weekend transfer blackouts, direct transfers without correspondent banks, and fast settlement rails. Stablecoins also limit the frustrations caused by opaque cross-border transactions, where fragmented compliance checks can leave legitimate payments in extended and unexplained limbo and without a path to clear or timely resolution.

Still, commercial banks have been reluctant to offer popular reserve-backed stablecoins from permissionless blockchains to their customers despite their retail popularity. That’s because they come with numerous challenges to smooth and secure operations: an uncertain regulatory status, compliance issues around anonymous accounts, gas fees, and the scalability limitations of layer 1 blockchain technology. But perhaps banks’ biggest concerns about stablecoins is that they create a problematic economic disconnect — giving customers access to reserve-backed stablecoins reduces reserves and, as a recent McKinsey study found, banks’ ability to lend.

As a result, many banks are trying to figure out how to offer their customers the benefits of stablecoins — high speed, low cost, 24/7 availability, and programmability — without introducing problems often associated with existing reserve-backed stablecoins, such as regulatory issues, poor throughput performance, negative influence on bank reserves, and potentially no yield participation.

Solution proposal

Realizing this vision means modernized payments architectures must seamlessly and instantly enable individuals and institutions to transfer bank-held assets to accounts at any target bank. Orchestrating this shared ecosystem requires central entities to establish the governing rulebook, enforce issuance limits, and manage network-wide settlement parameters. During its pilot, Crypto Finance assumed this role, which within GCUL is known as the “currency operator.”

In this position, Crypto Finance can configure the network for either instant or deferred settlement. This choice is analogous to traditional banking: instant settlement acts like real-time gross settlement, where transactions settle individually and immediately and require high liquid reserves. In contrast, deferred settlement operates like netting, where payments are accumulated and offset and only periodically settle the net difference. For the pilot, Crypto Finance chose to adopt deferred settlement, in which GCUL manifests capital efficiency. In this way, clients enjoy instant transfers while banks conserve liquidity through periodic settlement.

Concept validation

To demonstrate instant, bi-directional account-to-account transfers on GCUL, Crypto Finance orchestrated a pilot with two digital token issuers, a Swiss digital asset bank, and a Swiss B2B transaction bank. Crypto Finance established the rulebook for interactions between the participant banks, such as interbank settlement, integration with traditional SIC payment rails, and AML/compliance protocols. Although some backend steps still needed manual intervention, Crypto Finance’s pilot proved that fully automated, cross-institution integration is feasible and established a generalized architecture that can scale to virtually any asset class.

Robustness and performance

A temporary pilot is one thing; moving into live client transactions carrying legal liability brings a whole new set of operational challenges. Live payment rails are considered critical infrastructure that demands security and availability. GCUL addresses these needs through redundancy between geographically distributed nodes operating on an enterprise-grade consensus model, ensuring reliability. Deploying client workloads on Google Cloud provides that enterprise-grade foundation and allows financial institutions to pair the highly resilient GCUL network with secure-by-design infrastructure, encryption at rest and in transit, and robust access controls that satisfy many of banks’ common regulatory, privacy, and data sovereignty mandates. While some banks may consider integrating their systems with fully public and permissionless blockchains, this approach introduces severe regulatory hurdles, anonymity risks, unpredictable gas fees, and low throughput. These are all roadblocks that in the past would have significantly delayed the pilot or rendered it a non-starter.

Ease of integration

The pilot's implementation, with systems integration completed in under three months, was compartmentalized across dedicated Google Cloud projects per participant. The currency operator, Crypto Finance, connected specialized components to a dedicated GCUL API. The first was a role admin service that controls account managers and token managers on the network. Next, it implemented a settlement registry to record when periodic off-ledger settlement between participant banks has occurred once a predefined threshold is reached. Finally, a cloud key management service (KMS) stored the currency operator keys to sign transactions.

At the same time, participant banks connected their core banking systems to their own GCUL API instances. But these participant banks don’t need a large Google Cloud footprint. Instead, they can connect to GCUL nodes via Remote Procedure Call from their existing on-premise deployments and manage private key material through solutions other than KMS. Regardless of the setup, transactions are seamlessly routed to the shared global GCUL nodes.

Whether GCUL is exposed to a bank’s client or used merely as a bank backend is entirely at the integrating institution’s discretion. The banks participating in the pilot chose the latter, utilizing the ledger to upgrade their backend infrastructure. With GCUL under the hood, they improved intra-day transaction performance and provided customers with the user experience they were already accustomed to.

Regulatory compliance and governance by design

To join the Swiss Franc currency network on GCUL, participants must have regulatory licenses that let them perform third-party transfers and issue commercial bank money. Crucially, features like token and account management are not rigid network-wide limitations. Instead, they rely entirely on the currency operator and its specific rulebook. This standardizes fees, limits, settlement times, and technical configurations.

Managing counterparty risk is central to this governance. Rather than relying on unscalable bilateral agreements or complex clearinghouse default waterfalls, GCUL mitigates risk through these currency operator-enforced issuance limits.

It’s important to distinguish GCUL’s broader feature set from the concrete pilot setup. In the pilot, both participating banks operated with conservative initial limits based on their credit ratings in order to safely prove the architecture. But beyond the pilot, the network frees up capital by periodically netting outstanding obligations, which frees banks from having to fund and settle every transaction.

Looking ahead, risk management can be further innovated. One clever future enhancement would be to allow participants to dynamically increase their issuance limits by committing digital assets as collateral in segregated accounts, using solutions like Crypto Finance’s AnchorNote pledging solution. These assets could then be used to instantly settle outstanding street-side obligations, virtually eliminating counterparty risk without tying up traditional liquidity reserves.

The future

While Crypto Finance’s pilot was designed to focus on domestic commercial bank money transfers in Switzerland, GCUL's programmable architecture and high-performance smart contract language, GCULpy, are paving the way for deeper innovation. As institutions like Crypto Finance scale their use of GCUL, the network can expand to support real-time cross-currency settlement, automated foreign exchange, and dynamic collateral management involving tokenized digital assets. And looking further ahead, this infrastructure has laid the groundwork for next-generation financial services that range from point-of-sale payments to autonomous, AI-driven agentic payments.

The pilot proved that deploying high-performance, blockchain-based payment rails doesn’t mean compromising on strict regulatory compliance or core banking stability. By combining the high-throughput of GCUL with a secure, API-driven integration architecture, commercial banks can offer stablecoin-like speed to their customers while seamlessly preserving their capital efficiency. Ultimately, this compliant-by-design approach targets the operational bottlenecks of traditional finance while mitigating the inherent risks and complexities of public blockchains.

To learn how your institution can build on this blueprint to fundamentally upgrade your operational payments infrastructure, contact Google Cloud Sales to explore the Google Cloud Universal Ledger.

The team would also like to thank Phil Dettwiler, Andras Miklos, Ignazio Pollina, and Ozan Kizildogan at Crypto Finance and Googlers Chris Esch, Ishan Singh, Olena Clayton, and Stathis Onasoglou for their contributions.

entries.content:
Maire Newton

Outbound Product Manager, Google Cloud

Ramanan Balakrishnan

Group Outbound Product Manager, Data Cloud

As enterprises go from experimental AI agent prototypes to using them in production, data teams are realizing that access to data is not the same as understanding that data. To help bridge that gap, today, we are announcing the general availability (GA) of LookML semantic language indexing in Knowledge Catalog for Looker Core on Google Cloud.

To answer a complex business question accurately, an AI agent needs context — table schemas, data lineage, governance policies, business definitions, etc.. However, context is not a monolith; knowing where data lives is very different from knowing how to calculate metrics with it. In the enterprise, teams often conflate broad organizational context (usually in the form of metadata from structured and unstructured documents) with deterministic business semantics (the exact SQL formulas, join paths, and filtering rules that define metrics like net revenue or churn), assuming that a single data catalog or a business intelligence (BI) tool handling both enterprise-wide asset discovery and precise metric calculation.

In reality, no one tool can carry the entire load for agentic AI, as enterprise agents require both organizational context and deterministic business semantics. In Google Cloud environments, those are provided by Knowledge Catalog and LookML:

  • Broad enterprise context with Knowledge Catalog: Agents need a unified context graph that aggregates metadata across structured tables and unstructured documents. Through Knowledge Catalog, agents discover assets, inspect data quality, trace end-to-end lineage, respect column-level privacy tags, and surface corporate policy documents. The context graph tells an agent what data exists, how it is governed, and how it is connected.
  • Deterministic mathematical semantics with LookML: What a catalog does not author on its own is how the numbers are computed. Describing a table is not the same as defining how tables join or how metrics are calculated. Looker's modeling language, LookML, encodes production-tested semantic logic — multi-grain join protections, conditional filters, and exact KPI formulas — so agents don't guess SQL math at runtime.

With this native integration, the LookML business logic that powers your trusted BI reporting is automatically indexed into Knowledge Catalog — giving Gemini Enterprise and custom AI agents both enterprise-wide discovery and deterministic BI semantics.

Why a context graph needs deterministic semantics

When an LLM agent connects directly to raw database tables — even when armed with basic table descriptions or a business glossary — it still has to infer mathematical relationships on the fly. Without explicit semantic rules, agents routinely fall into two traps:

  • Metric definition drift: Standard text-to-SQL agents can invent conflicting formulas for foundational KPIs like net revenue or customer acquisition cost, failing to apply domain-specific accounting rules (such as recognizing revenue only when order_status = 'Complete' or prorating annual contracts across active service days).
  • Naive join fan-outs: Complex schemas often contain one-to-many (1:N) and zero-to-many (0:N) relationships across invoices, line items, and refunds. Without pre-modeled join relationships and symmetric aggregation rules, agent-generated SQL can multiply rows and inflate financial totals.

Knowledge Catalog and Looker solve this together, enabling you to model once in LookML and access those semantics everywhere across Google Cloud's AI ecosystem. Knowledge Catalog enforces semantic math when that logic is defined in a semantic modeling tool; LookML provides a mature, production-proven language for defining those exact mathematical relationships.

What's new: LookML in Knowledge Catalog

Previously, catalog integrations only captured shallow, file-level pointers and basic dashboard inventories. With this release, LookML's deterministic semantics become a first-class layer in the Knowledge Catalog context graph. An agent that finds a metric in the graph now also finds its exact definition, its join path, and its lineage back to source tables — in the same place, under the same governance. Synchronization is always on by default with no action required from end users, and with live sync, any update pushed to production LookML is reflected in Knowledge Catalog in near-real-time so agents operate on the freshest business logic.

Because this metadata is indexed directly into Knowledge Catalog by default, it is immediately available to Gemini Enterprise, without custom agent code or separate catalog data stores. When connected to Knowledge Catalog, Gemini Enterprise uses built-in read-only skills and hybrid search to look up technical schemas, business glossaries, and indexed LookML logic in a single step, passing that rich context directly to your federated BigQuery connector to generate accurate SQL. (For developers building custom agents, the same context bundles are also accessible via the LookupContext API.)

Knowledge Catalog now captures and links the following entity levels across Looker Core on Google Cloud:

  • LookML models (looker-model): Captures descriptive metadata, database connection routing, include hierarchies, data validation tests (assert), and parent-child EntryLinks mapping models to their associated Explores, Views, and LookML dashboards.
  • LookML Explores (looker-explore): Indexes full relational join logic (type, sql_on, relationship cardinality such as many_to_one fan-out protection, foreign_key, required_joins, and sql_where) as Schema-Join relationships. It also captures mandatory filter guardrails (always_filter, access_filter), inherited dimensions and measures, and predefined starter queries that help agents and analysts overcome the cold-start problem.
  • LookML Views and fields (looker-view): Extracts column-level compiled LookML SQL expressions (for example, ${total_revenue} / NULLIF(${count}, 0)), primary keys, dimension group timeframes, field synonyms, and derived table transformation logic (including SQL and native derived tables, partition keys, and cluster keys).
  • Dashboards, Looks, and tiles (looker-dashboard, looker-dashboard-element, looker-look): Catalogs both UI-created and LookML-defined dashboards and visualization tiles, complete with dashboard filters, chart types, ownership, and usage statistics. Users in Knowledge Catalog are able to see table- and column-level lineage from underlying BigQuery tables all the way to individual dashboard tiles, allowing data engineers to evaluate schema changes proactively, before disruptions occur.

Looker Core on Google Cloud automatically indexes resolved LookML models, Explores, Views, lineage, and dashboards directly into Knowledge Catalog.

Three patterns for data agents

Bringing LookML into Knowledge Catalog gives Gemini Enterprise (and your broader agent ecosystem) a single place to retrieve both broad organizational context and governance from Knowledge Catalog and explicit mathematical relationships and SQL definitions authored in LookML.

To see the impact of combining these two layers in Gemini Enterprise, compare how three architectures handle a complex cross-domain prompt: "What was our total revenue last fiscal quarter by product category, and which regional promotional policy limits apply?"

When you follow pattern 3 and pair Knowledge Catalog with Looker's semantic layer in an enterprise agent workflow, the agent moves from guessing at raw SQL to a governed, two-stage execution flow:

  • Context and governance discovery in Knowledge Catalog: Before touching any data, the agent searches Knowledge Catalog, verifies that the thelook_ecommerce LookML model is gold-certified, checks column-level governance tags, and maps the prompt to exact LookML dimensions and measures, converting natural language into structured business intent.
  • Deterministic semantic execution: Rather than having the LLM invent SQL on the fly, the agent grounds its SQL in LookML's exact mathematical definitions indexed in Knowledge Catalog and returns trusted, repeatable figures.

Alongside the answer, the agent returns an interactive Open in Looker Explore link with the exact measures and filters pre-populated, letting users slice, dice, and inspect row-level line items in a single click.

Side-by-side comparison of a baseline agent querying BigQuery directly (left), which guesses at raw SQL and fiscal dates, versus an agent governed by Knowledge Catalog and Looker (right), which applies indexed LookML definitions and returns an interactive "Open in Looker Explore" link.

Scaling agents for BI and the enterprise

A common question from data leaders is: "If we use Looker Conversational Analytics, when do we use an enterprise agent grounded in Knowledge Catalog?"

The two experiences are designed for complementary jobs across your organization:

  • Looker Conversational Analytics is your dedicated BI assistant: When business users are working inside BI workflows and asking questions scoped to a focused set of curated Looker Explores, Conversational Analytics delivers immediate, self-service data exploration and visualization directly within Looker.
  • Knowledge Catalog + Looker powers your enterprise-wide agents: When users ask questions in Gemini Enterprise across federated Data Cloud sources like BigQuery, they often span structured tables, BI metrics, and unstructured documents. Enabling Knowledge Catalog in Gemini Enterprise gives the assistant built-in skills to dynamically discover relevant semantics across hundreds of LookML models, pass indexed LookML join definitions, metric SQL formulas, and starter queries to the BigQuery connector to prevent join hallucinations, and enforce centralized governance aspects and IAM.

Getting started

Because Looker Core on Google Cloud, Knowledge Catalog, and Gemini Enterprise are natively integrated, you can connect your existing LookML business logic to your enterprise AI assistant in just a few clicks, with no custom agent code required.

To start discovering Looker semantics and grounding your agents:

  • Confirm first-party metadata indexing is enabled for Looker Core on Google Cloud. This is enabled by default for new instances, with no additional charge for storing Looker technical metadata. Once enabled, metadata synchronization into Knowledge Catalog is always on by default (across both initial indexing and ongoing live updates). Enable the Cloud Dataplex API and Data Lineage API in your project and grant users the required view roles (roles/dataplex.viewer, roles/looker.schemaViewer, and roles/datalineage.viewer) to have your resolved LookML models, Explores, Views, join paths, and dashboards automatically sync into Knowledge Catalog.
  • Enable Knowledge Catalog in Gemini Enterprise. When you attach a BigQuery (or Spanner, Cloud SQL, or AlloyDB) data store in federated query mode to your Gemini Enterprise app, the Knowledge Catalog integration is enabled automatically. You can also turn it on or off at any time in the Google Cloud console by opening your Gemini Enterprise app, navigating to Configurations > Assistant, toggling on Enable Knowledge Catalog, and clicking Save and publish.
  • Ask questions. Gemini Enterprise connects to Knowledge Catalog using end-user credentials, meaning users only discover and query data assets they have IAM permission to view (such as roles/bigquery.dataViewer). Behind the scenes, the assistant automatically looks up your indexed LookML definitions, join logic, and starter queries in Knowledge Catalog and passes them to your federated connector to deliver accurate, governed answers.

To dive deeper, read the Manage Looker Core on Google Cloud with Knowledge Catalog documentation and learn how to Connect to Knowledge Catalog in Gemini Enterprise. To build a more customized experience, explore our hands-on ADK agent codelab on GitHub.

Today, we’re announcing the general availability of an Anthropic-managed deployment option for Claude Models on Google Cloud. This gives teams more choice in how they run their models, helping them consolidate AI workloads on Google Cloud alongside our existingGoogle-managed deployment option.

Both options deliver the same frontier models on day zero, the same pricing, and the same Google Cloud billing. The difference comes down to who acts as your data processor and whether you need access to the new Claude platform features when they launch:

[NEW] Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed)

Anthropic operates the stack as the data processor on Google Cloud infrastructure under Anthropic’s terms of service, while organizations authenticate with Google Cloud IAM, maintain Cloud Audit Logging, and consolidate spend under their existing Google Cloud billing and eligible commitments.

entries.title: Introducing new self-learning context enrichment in Knowledge Catalog
entries.summary: Today, we’re launching self-learning context enrichment (preview) and a reimagined Knowledge Studio experience (preview) in Knowledge Catalog, Google Cloud’s context engine for agents. Building on Knowledge Catalog's existing Gemini-powered enrichment, self-learning enrichment analyzes agent and user interactions to find gaps and keep your business context accurate and current. Knowledge Studio is
entries.content:
Firat Elbey

Group Product Manager, Data Analytics

Vasiya Krishnan

Product Lead

Today, we’re launching self-learning context enrichment (preview) and a reimagined Knowledge Studio experience (preview) in Knowledge Catalog, Google Cloud’s context engine for agents. Building on Knowledge Catalog's existing Gemini-powered enrichment, self-learning enrichment analyzes agent and user interactions to find gaps and keep your business context accurate and current. Knowledge Studio is the new command center for context engineers and data stewards to explore their data estate conversationally, navigate a visual context graph, and review proposed changes to the context graph before they are published to their users and agents.

An agent is only as good as the organization-wide definitions, rules, and relationships it reasons over — the context, as it were. That’s why curating context has become one of the most important disciplines in enterprise agentic capabilities. Today, most of that work happens by hand. Context engineers write prompts and mappings agent by agent, while data stewards try to manually keep definitions current across thousands of assets. But this breaks down as organizations move from a handful of agents to thousands, and eventually millions.

Knowledge Catalog’s Gemini-powered self-learning enrichment turns that manual upkeep into a continuous feedback loop. By analyzing agent and user interactions, it pinpoints missing or outdated context and pulls verified definitions from playbooks, code repositories, and business documents into governed, reusable context sets. Then, with optimized search, every agent gets precisely the right context it needs instead of reasoning over bloated prompts and raw schemas, and benefits from shared learning across your organization. Knowledge Catalog makes AI agents nearly 4X more accurate, with up to 33% lower latency, and using up to 75% fewer tokens, based on internal benchmarks.

Keep context current with Gemini-powered self-learning enrichment

Consider a simple question to a Gemini agent: "What was the net revenue in EMEA last quarter?" Answering it correctly requires knowing how your company defines net revenue, which tables hold the bookings, and how they join, yet that knowledge is typically scattered across a finance playbook in Google Docs, a data model in GitHub, and a Confluence page. Static catalogs expect subject matter experts to manually capture and update business definitions, metrics, and other context upfront so that an agent can effectively query the right data. However, in reality, experts rarely have the time to document every asset, and the moment the finance team revises how partner credits are treated next quarter, static definitions fall behind and every agent with a hardcoded formula starts giving the wrong answer.

Knowledge Catalog’s enrichment capability acts where you already keep your business knowledge: across your team’s every doc, repo, and table. It connects to your structured data across first-party and third-party sources and unstructured data in Cloud Storage, Google Workspace, GitHub, Confluence, and SharePoint. It finds, extracts, assembles, and maintains that business knowledge for you, linking those unstructured sources like playbooks and wikis and their context to your structured metadata in Knowledge Catalog like tables and schemas to make your structured data far more discoverable and actionable. On demand or on a schedule, it proposes business definitions, table and column descriptions, join relationships, golden queries, and task-specific agent instructions, each with source citations and a confidence score. On every run, it detects what changed at the source, retires obsolete definitions, and flags conflicts for review.

It learns from both your user and agent interactions. You can configure enrichment to analyze interaction traces from Gemini agents, Conversational Analytics in BigQuery, or your custom agents while redacting PII, and it pinpoints where agents struggled, such as ambiguous column lookups, ungrounded metrics, missing definitions, or users rephrasing the same question. It then finds the authoritative answer and stages a fix, so the same mistake doesn't happen twice. That's how context engineering keeps pace with millions of agent interactions, freeing experts to review changes instead of writing them from scratch.

Configuring an enrichment task with connected sources, evaluation, and self-learning

Automation doesn't mean giving up control. You can choose to enable or disable auto-publishing at any time, and set the exact confidence score (for example, 85%) at which proposed changes are automatically approved. Anything below your threshold, along with sensitive updates such as deletions, become a Change Request for a steward to approve, edit, or reject. You can also provide your own evaluation set to test proposed updates end to end. Every change is logged with full provenance and can be reverted. And of course, Google never uses your data to train its models.

Reviewing enrichment proposals, confidence scores, and change diffs before publishing

Set the right context for each audience with context sets

By design, an enterprise context graph is quite broad, but for a given task, both agents and users often only need the right, trusted segment of it. Knowledge Catalog achieves that with context sets — curated, governed subsets of the context graph that contains the definitions, metrics, join logic, and golden queries for a specific domain, team, agent, or group of end users. For instance, a sales agent can be bound to the Sales context set, while a finance analyst's assistant can be bound to the Finance context set. Because "net revenue" can legitimately mean different things to each group, every domain maintains its own definitions in the same catalog. However, agents don't have to be bound to a single set; with search in Knowledge Catalog, an agent can also dynamically search and find the right context set for any given task.

Context sets also provide built-in data governance and fine-grained access control. Access to each context set is managed with IAM, so stewards decide which agents and users can read, use, or edit it. Agents only retrieve context from the sets they're authorized to use, and access to the underlying data continues to follow your existing permissions. Every update is traceable, and reversible, and because context sets build on the Open Knowledge Format (OKF), you can import an OKF bundle to become a context set and export it back out as OKF so your context stays portable.

Approved enrichments published to a governed context set

Explore and govern it all in Knowledge Studio

All of these capabilities come together in the reimagined Knowledge Catalog experience, built for context engineers and data stewards who curate and govern context for agents.

Navigating the context graph visually in Knowledge Studio

The new Knowledge Studio turns Knowledge Catalog from a repository of static inventory into an interactive command center, allowing you to:

  • See context coverage at a glance: Navigate a visual map of your cross-cloud data estate, from operational databases and warehouses to semantic models, context sets, and documentation.
  • Explore context conversationally: Ask business questions in natural language, traverse relationships across your enterprise context graph, and see exactly how agents reason over your metadata.
  • Review and validate enrichments in one place: Inspect each proposed change, source citations, and confidence score. Test context sets against real questions, and approve, edit, or roll back change requests with software-style version control.
  • Monitor enrichment runs: Track each enrichment task's schedule, results, token usage, and run duration, and get notified by email when a run completes.

Get started

These features will be rolled out to customers in the next few weeks. Sign up to request immediate access and visit the documentation for step-by-step guidance.

entries.content:
Ramanathan Venkatapathy

Distinguished Engineer

Rohit Jnagal

Distinguished Engineer

Every decade or so, a shift in software forces us to rethink computer architecture from first principles. After the first boom of web-scale traffic, Google pioneered warehouse-scale computing and Linux containers on Borg. This reshaped how we run internal workloads and ultimately sparked the modern cloud-native ecosystem through Kubernetes. A decade later, when deep learning models outgrew their compute and power needs, we went back to the drawing board and created Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). And as cloud security demanded stronger, hardware-rooted guarantees, we built Titanium, a custom silicon and Infrastructure Processing Unit (IPU) architecture that offloads I/O virtualization, storage, and cryptographic trust from the host CPU.

Today, we are in the middle of the next foundational shift: the transition to agentic AI that goes beyond answering questions and to taking action.

Across Google, AI agents are writing and executing code, running tools, driving browsers, orchestrating enterprise workflows, and iterating on software repositories. In a remarkably short span of time, agentic workloads have grown into one of the fastest-expanding consumers of compute and storage across our fleet.

Traditional compute primitives are not built for running hundreds of millions of these agents at planet scale at the required cost and latency. A new form factor is needed, which led us to build Agent Compute Engine, a new Google Cloud service that gives every AI agent its own hardware-isolated microVM with container-speed and zero credentials held inside the sandbox. 

In this blog, we discuss the problems that we encountered when trying to use existing paradigms to run agentic workloads at scale, and how we solved those foundational systems problems at every layer of the stack.

Running agents with traditional compute

The Gemini team set a simple-sounding goal. Every Gemini user would get a personal agent that runs in the cloud, remembers their work, and acts for them while they are away. To do that, each agent needed its own computer, with a filesystem, language runtimes, a browser, and network access.

Around the same time, the Gemini for business team set out to let companies build agents for their employees. Those agents needed to read Workspace documents, query internal databases, and call services inside a company’s private network.

Both teams split each agent into two parts. The harness, or “brain,” calls the model and decides what to do next. The sandbox, or “hands,” runs the code, shell commands, and browser that the model asks for. Each team writes and trusts its own harness. Giving a model hands with which to interact with the digital world means giving every agent its own computer, i.e., a real environment with a filesystem, language runtimes, network tools, and a browser.

Traditional VMs give you full control over the operating system, networking and storage, with a hypervisor-enforced isolation boundary, and they can run almost anything, from web applications to game servers to databases. That flexibility has a cost. Each VM boots and configures a full machine, so starting, suspending and resuming one takes seconds to minutes. Agents start, pause and resume constantly, so that overhead adds up.

The container world that we pioneered at Google is wonderfully fast and lightweight, because containers share the host operating system kernel. The extreme agility works perfectly for agentic workloads. But there are multiple examples like coding agents and developer assistants that need complete isolation as well as kernel- and root-level control of the agentic environment.

More importantly, understanding what an agent is trying to do is critical to efficiently handle the load. Even when an agent is idle between model steps, it needs to be able to quickly act when a new step is activated. It might also hold a critical working state. Tearing down the environment on every turn destroys the agent's working state and forces a slow rebuild on the next message. Provisioning a black-box, dedicated, always-on VM for every waiting agent wastes massive amounts of resources and limits what is possible.

We needed both the isolation of a VM and the speed and density of a container. We also needed a system that knows when an agent is working and when it is waiting.

Handling Google's planet-scale agentic workloads

We built Agent Compute Engine from first principles as a unified, agent compute platform for Google. Rather than handing product teams raw infrastructure primitives, the platform offers a simple microVM abstraction to rapidly provide a persistent, hardware-isolated computer.

This architecture is built to power four major classes of workloads across Google:

  • Interactive consumer and enterprise agent surfaces: Conversational chats that write and run code on the fly, interactive shell environments, and headless browser sandboxes that navigate the web and perform actions on a user's behalf.

  • Autonomous software engineering workspaces: Persistent, full-featured Linux computers with root access, compilers, and language servers that stay with a developer or coding agent across days or weeks of multi-step refactoring.

  • Massive-scale evaluations and reinforcement learning (RL): Frontier model training and benchmarking pipelines that spin up, branch, and evaluate thousands of parallel environment trajectories at high velocity.

  • Lightweight sandbox backends for Google services: A common execution environment that lets internal Google applications safely run dynamic logic and user-driven actions without building bespoke sandboxing stacks.
